summary: Collects into one place the requirements for Relying Party software in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), which are scattered across several RFCs. This makes it easier for implementers to find them, and the document is meant to be updated over time. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A rulebook for software that checks routing ID papers was scattered over many chapters. This document gathers every rule into one place so builders don't miss any.

subtitle: A single reference for all the rules RPKI relying party software must follow.

tldr.problem: Requirements for RPKI Relying Party software are scattered across 13 different RFCs, making it hard for implementers to ensure they have covered everything.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects all those requirements into one document, organized by the main tasks an RP must perform: fetching and caching data, verifying certificates, processing signed objects, and distributing results.
tldr.outcome: Implementers now have a single reference point to understand what RPKI RP software must do, though the document is intended to be updated as other RFCs change.

today: RFC 8897 is an Informational document that serves as a living reference for RPKI RP implementers. It consolidates requirements scattered across multiple RFCs and is intended to be updated as those RFCs are updated or as new RFCs are written.

sections.title: What RPKI Relying Parties Do
sections.content:
RPKI Relying Party software is used by network operators to download and verify Internet Number Resource (INR) data from the RPKI repository system. This verified data tells routers which Autonomous Systems (ASes) are authorized to originate routes for IP address prefixes, and which routers are authorized to sign BGP updates on behalf of specified ASes.

Because RPKI requirements are split across 13 different RFCs, it is easy for implementers to miss important rules. This document consolidates all requirements into one place and organizes them into four main categories: fetching and caching, certificate processing, signed object processing, and distributing results to BGP speakers.
sections.plainLanguage: RPKI RP software downloads and checks security papers that prove which companies can announce which internet addresses. These papers come from different sources and need different checks. This document says what all those checks are.

sections.title: Building and Maintaining the Cache
sections.content:
RP software uses mechanisms like rsync or RRDP (RFC 8182) to download RPKI objects from the repository and maintain a local cache. Each RP chooses its own set of trust anchors (TAs), typically the IANA and the five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs).

The RP discovers where to fetch objects by reading Trust Anchor Locators (TALs) and by using the Subject Information Access (SIA) and Authority Information Access (AIA) extensions in certificates. The RFC specifies requirements for handling key rollover (when old keys expire and new ones take over) and algorithm transition (as the cryptographic algorithms in use change over time). Efficient cache maintenance requires regular synchronization with the repository publication points.
sections.plainLanguage: RP software needs to download security papers from the internet regularly. It learns where to find them from special locator files and certificate fields. It has to know how to handle when security keys change or new types of math are used for checking signatures.

sections.title: Verifying Certificates and Data
sections.content:
RPKI uses X.509 certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs), but with a special profile defined in RFC 6487. The key difference is the mandatory use of an IP Address Delegation extension (from RFC 3779) that binds IP address resources to certificates.

When verifying a certificate, RP software must check that it conforms to the RPKI profile, that the Internet Number Resources (INRs) claimed by the issuer encompass those of the subject, and that the cryptographic signature is valid. When processing CRLs, the RP must verify that only the allowed extensions are present (AuthorityKeyIdentifier and CRLNumber) and that each CRL is signed with the public key of its issuing CA. If a CRL is inconsistent with the corresponding manifest, local policy determines how the RP should handle it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RP checks that all the security papers are real by verifying the signature with the issuer's keys. It also checks that a parent company's claim to own certain internet addresses is bigger than what it gives to a child company. It checks that papers that should have been revoked really are marked as revoked.

sections.title: Processing Signed Objects
sections.content:
The RPKI uses several types of signed objects, each with its own validation rules. Before processing any signed object, the RP must check basic syntax. Then it must perform type-specific checks:

Manifests (RFC 6486) list the objects that should be at a publication point; they help the RP detect missing or stale files. Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) state which ASes can originate routes for which IP prefixes. Ghostbusters Records provide contact information for the operator of a publication point. BGPsec Router Certificates bind public keys to routers and specify which ASes they represent. Each type has specific syntax and validation steps defined in the relevant RFC.

If a manifest is invalid or stale and the RP cannot get a fresher one, it contacts the publication point operator via Ghostbusters Records and applies local policy to decide whether to accept unsigned objects.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different kinds of signed papers: lists of what's supposed to be there, permits to announce routes, contact information for when something goes wrong, and keys for routers. Each kind has its own special checks that the RP must do.

sections.title: Sharing Results and Local Control
sections.content:
Once the RP has built and validated its cache, it shares the results with BGP speakers in the network. The protocols for this distribution are specified in RFC 6810 and RFC 8210. BGP speakers periodically request updated validated origin AS data and router/ASN data.

ISPs may also implement SLURM (Simplified Local Internet Number Resource Management with the RPKI; RFC 8416) to establish local overrides and exceptions to the global RPKI data. This allows network operators to protect routes from adverse actions or account for local routing policies that differ from the global RPKI data.
sections.plainLanguage: After checking everything, the RP sends the validated data to the routers that need it. Network operators can also set up local rules to override or add exceptions to the global security rules when needed for their own network.
